d3-case-assessment.brief: Meridian Health Network is building a cancer-detection imaging model: an algorithm does an initial pass over scans and routes anything below a confidence threshold to a radiologist for secondary review. Meridian has already defined its AI ethics principles, stood up a governance committee, assembled a cross-functional team and written its standards, workflows and risk-threshold policies. It plans to use a cloud provider for hosting, a consulting firm for development, its own patient data, and de-identified imaging licensed from a clinical research partner. You are the AIGP tasked with scoping the impact assessment that has to happen before training and testing begin — and with explaining, precisely, what that assessment is for and what it is not.
d3-case-assessment.steps[0].why: As a management tool, the impact assessment's job is to surface and control what could go wrong — bias, unsafe misclassification, patient harm — not to tally the upside Meridian already believes in. That's a narrower claim than what the assessment covers, though: the official IAPP guidance frames the assessment's *purpose* more broadly, as building understanding of both potential benefits and harms (FSG p.6/8, Q2). Both are correct at different altitudes — this step is about what the assessment is built to manage day to day, not the full scope of what it is meant to help Meridian understand. Roles/responsibilities and legal-risk-only framings are real governance artifacts, but they're not what this particular document does.
d3-case-assessment.steps[1].why: A privacy impact assessment is the best existing template to adapt because both instruments evaluate risk arising from how data is used — extending a PIA's methodology into ethical, social and legal AI-specific territory is more tractable than starting fresh. Safety and security assessments are narrower single-lens tools, and an environmental impact assessment addresses a question this document doesn't own at all.
d3-case-assessment.steps[2].why: Impact assessments center on risk to people, institutions and legal compliance — privacy, data provenance, bias — and for a narrow AI use case, energy consumption during processing sits outside that required core, even though it's a legitimate topic in broader AI-sustainability conversations. Privacy impact, data-source lawfulness and output bias are all standard, required content regardless of how narrow the system is.
d3-case-assessment.steps[3].why: Performing the impact assessment pre-training surfaces discrimination risk while there is still time to change data sourcing, labeling or design — that's the whole point of doing it early rather than after the fact. More data doesn't fix a poorly scoped problem, a third-party audit and a bias bounty are both post-hoc detection mechanisms that assume the model already exists.

d3-case-drift-alarm.brief: It's 4:50pm on a Friday. Finnovate's automated loan-underwriting model has been in production for six months, making thousands of decisions a day. A governance dashboard alert fires: F1 score has dropped sharply, and a statistical test shows the live input distribution has diverged from the training distribution. Buried in the same alert stream, a slower-burning signal has also been building for months: a demographic-bias check shows a 1.8% disparity in approval rates for a protected class — under Finnovate's 2% escalation threshold, but trending upward. You're the governance lead on call. What you do in the next hour, and the next month, is being logged.
d3-case-drift-alarm.steps[0].why: With a live, drifting model actively making loan decisions, the first move has to stop the bleeding — pull it from production and fall back to a manual process before anything else happens. Root-cause analysis is essential but not while the model is still deciding real applications; automated retraining on the same drifting data risks baking the problem in deeper; and a public statement before containment and investigation is premature and gets the sequence backwards.
d3-case-drift-alarm.steps[1].why: Incident response sequencing puts containment first precisely because Finnovate's model is still actively harming applicants with every decision it makes — you stop the damage before you diagnose it. Investigation is necessary but second; leading with external communication or with recovery-to-prior-state without first stopping the live harm both skip the step that actually protects people right now.
d3-case-drift-alarm.steps[2].why: A numeric threshold is a floor for routine monitoring, not a ceiling on judgment — governance is expected to escalate protected-class impact even when the number technically falls short, because that's the more defensible posture if a regulator later asks why a known disparity sat unaddressed. Waiting for the number to cross 2%, waiting for a scheduled forum, or handling it quietly with compensating controls all treat the threshold as permission to wait, which is exactly the exposure this rule exists to close.
d3-case-drift-alarm.steps[3].why: Formal logging is the immediate governance step that triggers everything downstream — investigation, stakeholder notification, corrective and preventive action — and a blameless retrospective that still assigns responsibility for fixes is how the findings turn into durable process change rather than a one-off patch. Jumping to retraining or closing the ticket once the dashboard looks fine skips the auditable record; delaying stakeholder notice until after CAPA reverses an order governance depends on (SG).

d3-case-precode.brief: Harborline Credit is a regional lender that wants to automate first-pass creditworthiness scoring for small-business loans. The idea has momentum — the CEO saw a competitor's press release and wants "an AI thing" running by next quarter. You are the AI governance lead brought in before a single model is trained, tasked with making sure the project starts from a defensible business case rather than a demo. Two junior architects have already sketched a neural-network design on a whiteboard; a data scientist is quietly assembling a training set from an old marketing database. Your job this week is to slow the room down enough to do planning in the right order — objective, context, governance approach and stakeholders first, technical choices after — before any of that whiteboard sketch becomes real spend.
d3-case-precode.steps[0].why: Planning opens with the business case: why AI, and why now, before any risk, redress or technical question can even be scoped sensibly. TEVV and impact assessments are real governance steps, but they evaluate a system that has already been defined; redress feasibility matters once you know the use case will proceed. Skipping straight to those questions without first justifying the project itself is planning out of order.
d3-case-precode.steps[1].why: A comprehensive cost-benefit analysis has to weigh societal impacts alongside the balance sheet, or Harborline is optimizing for approval speed while blind to who the model systematically screens out. The other three options are exactly the narrow, ROI-only framing the CEO already brought in the door — restating them doesn't fix the gap, it names it.
d3-case-precode.steps[2].why: Planning scopes objectives, assumptions, context and governance approach — not model architecture. Choice of architecture (neural network vs. decision tree vs. something else) is a design-phase decision made once planning has defined what the system needs to do. A near-identical practice item keys governance approach as the planning exclusion instead — that variant conflicts with the BoK's lifecycle module and is not followed here; 's architecture-is-excluded framing is the one this desk teaches.
d3-case-precode.steps[3].why: Stakeholder mapping exists to weight risk assessment toward whoever bears the AI system's consequences most directly — for Harborline, that's the applicants whose access to credit the model decides, not the teams who built it or the leadership who approved it. Technical, compliance and executive perspectives all matter and all have a seat, but none of them absorbs the direct impact the way an applicant who gets wrongly declined does.
d3-case-precode.steps[4].why: Algorithm-type selection is a technical judgment call that belongs with the people who understand the data, the clinical or business context and the performance requirements in depth — Harborline's own data science team, not an outside vendor. The governance committee sets the risk envelope the algorithm has to operate within, but picking the specific technique is not a governance-committee function — don't confuse this with step 3's ruling that architecture belongs in design rather than planning; this step is about *who* makes a design-phase call, not *when* it's made. A cloud provider or consulting firm can advise, but the decision authority sits with Harborline's own team.

d3-case-release.brief: GlobalCart is weeks from launching "Echo," a proprietary large language model that will answer customer queries, process returns and handle simple escalations. Legal is worried about liability; PR is worried about brand damage if Echo says something biased or wrong. Before Echo goes live, your job is to determine whether it is actually ready — using shadow-mode results, the right documentation artifact for the right audience, and a clear line between what gets published to customers and what stays internal.
d3-case-release.steps[0].why: Shadow-mode testing with documented outcomes is release-readiness evidence precisely because it exposes the model to real traffic and real edge cases without the downside of a live failure — it's the AI-governance equivalent of parallel testing in disaster-recovery planning. A high-performing model with no documented metrics proves nothing to an auditor, outsourcing testing without internal review abdicates governance's own job, and a press release is a marketing act, not evidence of anything (SG).
d3-case-release.steps[1].why: Intended use and limitations define the boundary of where Echo can be responsibly deployed — deploying outside that boundary is one of the most common roots of governance failure and liability exposure, which is exactly what legal is worried about. Performance metrics and training-data details are real content in the same document but carry no governance weight if the model gets used outside its validated scope, and energy consumption is a sustainability concern, not the top release-readiness risk here.
d3-case-release.steps[2].why: The two artifacts are scoped differently on purpose: the model card is anchored to one specific model version and answers "what is this model and how should it be used," while the system dossier answers "how does this fit into the production system as a whole," including monitoring and conformity evidence the model card explicitly does not restate. Treating them as duplicates, splitting them by internal/public audience, or splitting them by metrics-vs-data all misdescribe the actual boundary (SG).
d3-case-release.steps[3].why: Public disclosures owe customers purpose, legal compliance and honest limitations — not GlobalCart's trade secrets. Proprietary methods stay internal; disclosure requirements balance public understanding against the organization's legitimate interest in protecting its IP, so intended purpose, legal compliance and stated limitations are exactly what belongs in the disclosure while the underlying technique does not.
d3-case-release.steps[4].why: Retraining resets how the model actually makes decisions, so governance treats the retrained model as a new release, not a patch — full re-validation, updated documentation and transparency artifacts, and formal sign-off before it touches production again. This is a different rule from Case D's containment-first sequencing: Case D says don't retrain (or do anything else) *before* a live incident is contained; this step says that once retraining does happen — incident-triggered or routine — it owes first-release rigor on the way back out, not a shortcut because the model already shipped once (SG).
